title: Simple-root cones are chambers with a simply transitive reflection action
statement: Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space [def-weil-vector-space-dimension], equipped with a positive definite symmetric bilinear form $(\ ,\ )$. Let $R\subseteq V\setminus\{0\}$ be finite, span $V$, and satisfy $R\cap\mathbf R\alpha=\{\alpha,-\alpha\}$ for each $\alpha\in R$. Assume that the orthogonal reflection $s_\alpha(x)=x-2(x,\alpha)(\alpha,\alpha)^{-1}\alpha$ permutes $R$ and that $2(\beta,\alpha)(\alpha,\alpha)^{-1}\in\mathbf Z$ for all $\alpha,\beta\in R$. Write $W_R\subseteq\operatorname{GL}_{\mathbf R}(V)$ for the group generated by these reflections and $H_\alpha=\{x:(x,\alpha)=0\}$. A base $D\subseteq R$ is a real vector-space basis such that every root is an integral linear combination of $D$ with all coefficients nonnegative or all nonpositive. For each base $D$, put $R_D^+=R\cap\sum_{\alpha\in D}\mathbf Z_{\geq0}\alpha$ and $C_D=\{x\in V:(x,\alpha)>0\text{ for all }\alpha\in D\}$. Then $D\mapsto C_D$ is a bijection from bases to connected components of $V\setminus\bigcup_{\alpha\in R}H_\alpha$, called chambers, and $R_D^+=\{\beta\in R:(x,\beta)>0\}$ for every $x\in C_D$. The group $W_R$ acts simply transitively on chambers: for every ordered pair of chambers $(C,C')$ there is exactly one $w\in W_R$ with $wC=C'$. The bijection is equivariant: $wC_D=C_{wD}$. When $R=\varnothing$, the spanning assumption forces $V=0$, the empty base has chamber $V=\{0\}$, and $W_R=\{1\}$.

source.place: Appendix C.9--C.10, printed pp.609--610; C.21--C.22, printed p.612, via the real invariant-inner-product formulation of C.19--C.20, printed p.611.

proof.text: Write $U=V\setminus\bigcup_{a\in R}H_a$. Substitution in the reflection formula gives $s_a^2=1$ and $(s_ax,s_ay)=(x,y)$. Thus every $w\in W_R$ is orthogonal, permutes $R$, and satisfies $wH_a=H_{wa}$ and $ws_aw^{-1}=s_{wa}$ (substitute $w^{-1}x$ in the formula). Its permutation action on $R$ is faithful, since $R$ spans $V$. Hence $W_R$ is finite. If $R$ is empty, spanning gives $V=0$; the unique base is empty, $U=V=\{0\}$ is connected, and the reflection-generated group is trivial. All conclusions follow in this case; assume henceforth $R\ne\varnothing$.

source.place: C.8, p.609; C.15 and C.20, p.611; explicit reflection calculations and rank-zero case.

proof.text: For $t\in U$ put $P_t=\{a\in R:(t,a)>0\}$ and $A_t=\{x\in V:(x,a)>0\text{ for }a\in P_t,\ (x,a)<0\text{ for }a\in-P_t\}$. Here $R=P_t\sqcup(-P_t)$ because $R=-R$ and $t$ is regular. Every segment between points of $A_t$ stays in $A_t$, since each signed pairing is a positive convex combination of positive numbers; therefore $A_t$ is path connected and connected. On any connected subset of $U$, the sign of $(x,a)$ is constant: otherwise its intersections with the two open sets $(x,a)>0$ and $(x,a)<0$ separate that subset. The connected component of $t$ is consequently contained in $A_t$ and, by its maximality, contains the connected set $A_t$. Hence that component is exactly $A_t$, and $P_t$ depends only on it.

source.place: Appendix C.9, printed pp.609--610; explicit elementary details supplied by the worker.

proof.text: Fix $t\in U$ and let $S_t\subseteq P_t$ be the roots that are not sums of two roots of $P_t$. Every $b\in P_t$ is a sum of elements of $S_t$, with repetitions allowed. Indeed, induct over the finite set of positive values $(t,b)$ in increasing order. An indecomposable root already is such a sum. Otherwise $b=c+d$ for $c,d\in P_t$, and both $(t,c)$ and $(t,d)$ are strictly smaller than $(t,b)$; concatenate the sums given by induction. Thus every positive root is a nonnegative integral combination of $S_t$; every other root is its negative. Since $R$ spans $V$, so does $S_t$.

source.place: Appendix C.9, printed pp.609--610; explicit elementary details supplied by the worker.

proof.text: Distinct $a,b\in S_t$ satisfy $(a,b)\leq0$. To see this, suppose $(a,b)>0$. Reducedness and $a,b\in P_t$ imply they are not proportional. Set $m=2(a,b)/(b,b)$ and $n=2(a,b)/(a,a)$; these are positive integers. Positivity of $(a-\lambda b,a-\lambda b)$ at $\lambda=(a,b)/(b,b)$ gives $(a,b)^2<(a,a)(b,b)$, hence $mn<4$. Therefore $m=1$ or $n=1$. If $m=1$, $s_ba=a-b\in R$; if $n=1$, $s_ab=b-a\in R$, and negation again gives $a-b\in R$. Regularity of $t$ makes exactly one of $a-b$ and $b-a$ positive. The former gives $a=b+(a-b)$ and the latter $b=a+(b-a)$, contradicting indecomposability. This proves the inequality using only the reflection formula and integrality.

source.place: Appendix C.9, printed pp.609--610; explicit elementary details supplied by the worker.

proof.text: The vectors in $S_t$ are real linearly independent. Given a real relation, separate its strictly positive and strictly negative coefficients to write $u=\sum_{a\in I}c_a a=\sum_{b\in J}d_b b=v$, with $I,J$ disjoint and $c_a,d_b>0$. The preceding step gives $(u,v)\leq0$. Since $u=v$, positive definiteness forces $u=v=0$. But pairing with $t$ gives $(t,u)=\sum_{a\in I}c_a(t,a)>0$ if $I$ is nonempty, and likewise for $J$. Both sets must be empty. Thus $S_t$ is independent and spans, hence is a real basis; the integral decompositions of the preceding step make it a base. They also show $R^+_{S_t}=P_t$: positive roots are such sums, and any nonzero nonnegative sum of $S_t$ pairs positively with $t$.

source.place: Appendix C.9, printed pp.609--610; explicit elementary details supplied by the worker.

proof.text: For any base $D$, the linear map $x\mapsto((x,a))_{a\in D}$ is bijective: its kernel is zero by spanning and positive definiteness, and domain and codomain have equal finite dimension. Choose $x$ with all these pairings equal to $1$, so $C_D$ is nonempty. For $y\in C_D$, the same-sign integral expansion of a nonzero root gives $(y,b)>0$ exactly for $b\in R_D^+$. Thus $C_D=A_x$ and is a chamber. Conversely, for $t\in U$, the previous steps give a base $S_t$ with $C_{S_t}=A_t$. If $C_D=A_t$, every $d\in D$ is a nonnegative integral sum of $S_t$, whose members in turn have nonnegative integral $D$-coordinates. The coefficient vector of $d$ is a standard unit vector, so its expression as a sum of nonzero nonnegative integer vectors has just one summand. Thus $d\in S_t$, so $D\subseteq S_t$; both are bases and have the same cardinality, hence $D=S_t$. This proves the bijection and the asserted formula for $R_D^+$.

source.place: Appendix C.9, printed pp.609--610; explicit elementary details supplied by the worker.

proof.text: For a base $D$, put $P=R_D^+$. If $a\in D$ and $b\in P\setminus\{a\}$, some $D$-coefficient of $b$ other than its $a$-coefficient is positive, since otherwise reducedness would give $b=a$. Reflection changes only the $a$-coefficient. The resulting root $s_ab$ therefore has a positive coefficient and, as all root coefficients have one sign, lies in $P$. It is not $a$, because then $b=s_aa=-a$. Involutivity now gives $s_a(P\setminus\{a\})=P\setminus\{a\}$, while $s_aa=-a$. Also $wD$ is a base for every $w\in W_R$, and orthogonality gives $(wx,wa)=(x,a)$, so $wC_D=C_{wD}$.

source.place: C.21--C.22, p.612; coefficient calculation and equivariance.

proof.text: Fix chambers $C_D$ and $C'$, choose $h\in C_D$ and $y\in C'$, and choose $z=wy$ in the finite orbit $W_Ry$ maximizing $(z,h)$. If $(z,a)<0$ for some $a\in D$, then $$(s_az,h)-(z,h)=-2(z,a)(h,a)/(a,a)>0,$$ contradicting maximality. The point $z$ is regular, since the group permutes the hyperplanes, so all $(z,a)>0$ and $z\in C_D$. Since $w$ is a homeomorphism of $U$, it maps components to components; $wC'$ and $C_D$ meet at $z$, hence agree. Thus a reflection-group element carries either of these chambers to the other, proving transitivity.

source.place: C.10, p.610 and C.22, p.612; finite-orbit maximization supplies the transitivity argument.

proof.text: To prove freeness at $C_D$, [lem-sfb-simple-root-reflection-generation] applies to precisely the given real form, reduced crystallographic root set and base $D$. Hence any $w\in W_R$ has an expression $s_{a_1}\cdots s_{a_k}$ with $a_i\in D$; inverses are the same reflections. Take one of minimal length. If $wC_D=C_D$, then $wP=P$: for $x\in C_D$ and $b\in P$, $(wx,wb)=(x,b)>0$, and $wx\in C_D$; use the positive-root formula and finiteness for equality.

source.place: C.11, p.610, first assertion only; C.10 and C.22: preparation for the exchange argument.

proof.text: If the minimal length $k$ is positive, write $w=u s_a$ with $a=a_k\in D$. Since $wa\in P$ and $s_aa=-a$, one has $ua=-wa\in-P$. Apply [lem-sfb-root-sign-word-deletion] to the word $u$, the partition $R=P\sqcup(-P)$ and $b=a$. Its sign-preservation hypothesis is exactly step 7. The lemma gives a word for $u s_a=w$ obtained by deleting one factor of $u$, of length $k-2$, contradicting minimality (when $k=1$, its assertion that the empty word cannot send $a$ negative already gives the contradiction). Thus $k=0$ and $w=1$. Finally, if $w_1C=w_2C=C'$, the element $w_2^{-1}w_1$ stabilizes $C$ and equals $1$, so $w_1=w_2$. Combined with transitivity and equivariance, this proves every clause.

source.place: C.10, p.610; explicit exchange/deletion proof of freeness, rather than assuming the Coxeter presentation.
